title: What Really Happened at the First Thanksgiving
hook: Autumn 1621: ninety Wampanoag men walk toward a village of fifty survivors. What happened next became America's most famous meal, and most of what we picture is wrong.
thumbnail_picture: Big close-up on the right of a steaming roasted deer haunch and a wooden bowl of corn on a rough table, with a wide-eyed, amazed Pilgrim man in a dark wool coat and white collar staring at it, snowy wooden settlement blurred behind, left third empty, dramatic warm light
description:
What really happened at the first Thanksgiving in 1621? The true story of the Pilgrims at Plymouth, Massasoit, Tisquantum (Squanto), the Wampanoag alliance, what was actually on the table, and how Lincoln made Thanksgiving a national holiday in 1863.

Half the Pilgrims died in their first winter. A kidnapped man, a peace pact with a Wampanoag leader and a surprise visit by ninety Wampanoag men turned a harvest into the most famous meal in American history. Here's the real version, with no pumpkin pie.

Sources: Edward Winslow's 1621 letter, printed in Mourt's Relation (1622); William Bradford, Of Plymouth Plantation; Nathaniel Philbrick, Mayflower (2006); Plimoth Patuxet Museums; Abraham Lincoln's Thanksgiving Proclamation, October 3, 1863 (National Archives).
tags: what really happened at the first thanksgiving
what was eaten at the first thanksgiving

scenes.narration: Autumn, 1621. Ninety Wampanoag men walk out of the woods toward a tiny English village.
scenes.delivery: low, tense, like the start of a thriller
scenes.caption: PLYMOUTH, 1621
scenes.picture: A long line of Wampanoag men of 1621 with long black hair, deerskin leggings and fur mantles walking out of a golden autumn forest toward a few small thatched wooden houses behind a rough fence by the sea, seen from behind the men, wide shot, late afternoon light.

scenes.narration: Inside are barely fifty settlers, the survivors of a winter that buried half their people.
scenes.caption: THE QUESTION
scenes.picture: A handful of thin English settlers of 1621 in worn wool coats, white collars and wide-brimmed hats, a man, a woman and a child, standing in the doorway of a small thatched wooden house, staring out with worried faces, a few simple wooden grave markers on the hill behind them.

scenes.narration: What happens next becomes America's most famous meal. And almost everything you picture about it is wrong, starting with the pumpkin pie.
scenes.delivery: curious, with a small smile on the last words
scenes.caption: THE ANSWER
scenes.picture: A rough outdoor wooden table in a 1621 village set with roasted venison, wild ducks and bowls of corn, an English settler in a wide-brimmed hat and a Wampanoag man with long black hair and a fur mantle reaching for food side by side, autumn trees behind.

scenes.narration: It begins in September 1620, when a creaky ship called the Mayflower leaves England with 102 passengers.
scenes.caption: SEPTEMBER 1620
scenes.picture: The wooden sailing ship Mayflower with brown sails leaving an English harbour at dawn, families in plain dark clothes waving from a stone quay, grey-blue sea, gulls overhead

scenes.narration: Historians estimate they were crammed onto a shared deck about the size of a tennis court, for roughly two months.
scenes.caption: ABOUT 2 MONTHS AT SEA
scenes.picture: Cramped dim lower deck of a wooden ship, families in plain dark clothes squeezed together on blankets and barrels beside a swinging oil lantern, low wooden beams, tired faces

scenes.narration: Mid-ocean, a storm cracks a main beam. Panic. So they fix it with a big iron screw and keep going.
scenes.caption: STORM
scenes.picture: Two sailors and a man in a dark coat straining to lift a cracked wooden beam with a huge iron screw jack inside a pitching ship, lantern light, sea spray, scared faces

scenes.narration: They were aiming farther south. But they hit Cape Cod in November, with winter already closing in.
scenes.caption: CAPE COD
scenes.picture: The Mayflower anchored off a bleak sandy coast with dunes and bare scrub pine, cold overcast sky, a few settlers in dark coats crowding the ship's rail and staring at the shore

scenes.narration: So they settle at Plymouth in December, with freezing rain, no houses, and barely enough food.
scenes.caption: DECEMBER 1620
scenes.picture: Three English settler men in dark wool coats hammering a half-built timber hut on a muddy hillside in freezing rain, wet bare trees, a wooden ship in the grey bay behind

scenes.narration: Then people start coughing. Scurvy and lung infections, most likely pneumonia, tear through the ship and the half-built huts.
scenes.caption: THE SICKNESS
scenes.picture: Interior of a dim rough timber hut, a pale feverish English settler man lying under a blanket on a straw bed while a worried woman in a linen cap holds a wooden cup to his lips, faint candlelight

scenes.narration: At the worst point, only six or seven people are healthy enough to nurse everyone else.
scenes.caption: 6 OR 7 HEALTHY
scenes.picture: One exhausted English settler man in a dark wool coat carries a wooden bucket of water down the aisle of a long dim hut, sick people lying on straw on both sides, candlelight

scenes.narration: By spring, about half of them are dead.
scenes.delivery: solemn, a long beat before it
scenes.caption: HALF GONE
scenes.picture: Snowy hillside above a small wooden settlement, a row of simple wooden grave markers in the snow, one lone mourning woman in a dark cloak and linen cap standing beside them, grey dawn

scenes.narration: And they hide it. According to Bradford, they hid the graves, and tradition adds they sowed corn over them, so the Native people couldn't count the dead.
scenes.caption: HIDDEN GRAVES
scenes.picture: Two English settler men in dark wool coats pressing corn seeds into a flattened grave mound at dusk, one glancing nervously over his shoulder toward the dark edge of the woods

scenes.narration: But who was watching? Strangely, the land they'd picked looked ready for them: cleared fields, and nobody in sight.
scenes.caption: EMPTY LAND
scenes.picture: Wide view of overgrown cleared fields with old low planting mounds on a coastal hill above a quiet bay, no people, one English settler man in a dark wool coat standing at the edge, puzzled face

scenes.narration: Here's why. It was a village called Patuxet, and a few years earlier, disease had swept the coast and wiped it out.
scenes.caption: PATUXET
scenes.picture: Abandoned Wampanoag village of empty round bark-covered wigwams in a coastal clearing, silent and overgrown with tall grass, low mist, no people, grey morning light

scenes.narration: Nearby, the Wampanoag nation was reeling too. Many villages had lost most of their people, and rivals were circling.
scenes.caption: WAMPANOAG
scenes.picture: A Wampanoag village of bark-covered wigwams with only a few people left, a worried elder with grey hair in a deerskin mantle looking toward the distant forest, smoke rising, evening light

scenes.narration: Then, on March 16, 1621, by the old calendar they used, a man strides into Plymouth and says, in English, "Welcome, Englishmen."
scenes.caption: MARCH 16, 1621 (OLD STYLE)
scenes.picture: A tall Native man in deerskin leggings carrying a bow walks calmly between rough timber houses with one friendly open hand raised, startled English settlers in dark coats staring at him, early spring light

scenes.narration: His name is Samoset. He learned English from fishermen, and he says another man speaks it even better.
scenes.caption: SAMOSET
scenes.picture: Samoset, a Native man with black hair in a deerskin cloak, sitting by a fire inside a rough timber hut and talking with gestures, two curious English men in dark coats leaning in over a wooden table, warm firelight

scenes.narration: That man is Tisquantum, better known as Squanto. And his story explains why any of this worked.
scenes.caption: TISQUANTUM
scenes.picture: Portrait-style shot of Tisquantum, a lean Native man in his thirties with long black hair and a deerskin mantle, thoughtful strong face, standing on a Plymouth hillside with the bay behind him, spring morning

scenes.narration: Seven years earlier, an English captain had kidnapped him and others, planning to sell them as slaves in Spain.
scenes.caption: KIDNAPPED, 1614
scenes.picture: An English sailing ship near a sandy shore, Native men being forced by armed sailors in ragged coats into a rowboat, fear on their faces, grey sky, 1614

scenes.narration: Somehow he made it to England, then back across the Atlantic. In 1619, he finally walked home.
scenes.caption: HOME, 1619
scenes.picture: Tisquantum, a lean Native man with long black hair wearing a worn mix of deerskin and English wool, walks alone along a sandy coastal path toward a hill, a ship far out on the sea, hopeful face

scenes.narration: But home was gone. He found Patuxet empty, everyone he knew dead. A year later, English settlers built on its ruins.
scenes.caption: NOTHING LEFT
scenes.picture: Tisquantum, a lean Native man with long black hair in a worn deerskin mantle, standing alone in the middle of an empty ruined village of collapsed wigwams, shoulders low, grief on his face, grey light

scenes.narration: So why help them? Nobody knows for sure. But his village was gone, and these newcomers were now part of his world.
scenes.caption: WHY HELP?
scenes.picture: Tisquantum, a lean Native man with long black hair in a deerskin mantle, facing an English settler man in a dark wool coat across a split-rail fence at the edge of Plymouth, cautious curious expressions, spring afternoon

scenes.narration: Meanwhile, the Wampanoag leader, Massasoit, faced a risky choice: befriend strangers, or face his enemies alone.
scenes.caption: MASSASOIT
scenes.picture: Massasoit, a proud middle-aged Wampanoag leader with black hair, a shell necklace and a deerskin mantle, standing on a hill and looking toward a distant English settlement, serious thoughtful face

scenes.narration: He came to Plymouth with about sixty men. The Pilgrims, weak and outnumbered, could only hope he came in peace.
scenes.caption: THE MEETING
scenes.picture: A line of Wampanoag men in deerskin mantles walking up a path toward a small English settlement on a hill, a few nervous settlers in dark coats waiting beside a wooden hut, bright spring day

scenes.narration: He did. They shook on a deal: neither side would harm the other, and if one was attacked, the other would help.
scenes.caption: THE PEACE PACT
scenes.picture: Close-up of Massasoit, a proud middle-aged Wampanoag leader in a deerskin mantle with a shell necklace, clasping hands with an English leader in a dark wool coat inside a rough wooden room, firelight

scenes.narration: It bought the colony something it badly needed: time.
scenes.caption: TIME
scenes.picture: Calm Plymouth settlement in spring sunshine, children playing between timber houses and a woman in a linen cap hanging linen cloth on a line, green grass, blossoming trees

scenes.narration: But peace doesn't fill stomachs. English seeds were struggling in Plymouth's sandy soil.
scenes.caption: HUNGER
scenes.picture: A worried English farmer in a dark wool coat kneeling in thin pale sandy soil, holding a small wilted wheat sprout between his fingers, sparse weak seedlings in rows, windy day

scenes.narration: So Squanto shows them how to plant corn in hills, with a fish buried alongside the seed.
scenes.caption: FISH FERTILIZER
scenes.picture: Close-up of Tisquantum's brown hands burying a silvery fish next to corn seeds in a small mound of dark earth, an English settler man in a dark coat crouching beside him watching closely

scenes.narration: The fish rot into fertilizer. And Native farmers in the region often planted beans and squash right alongside the corn.
scenes.caption: CORN, BEANS, SQUASH
scenes.picture: A lush planted field of tall green corn with bean vines climbing the stalks and broad squash leaves covering the ground, sunny summer day, a wooden fence in the distance

scenes.narration: Better still, in spring, fish swarm up the brook by the thousands. A free fertilizer delivery, right to their doorstep.
scenes.caption: THE FISH RUN
scenes.picture: A shallow clear brook packed with silvery fish swimming upstream, English settlers in wool clothes and one Native man scooping fish into baskets on the muddy bank, spring light

scenes.narration: A single ear of corn can hold several hundred kernels. Plant enough hills, and a starving colony becomes a farm.
scenes.caption: HUNDREDS OF KERNELS
scenes.picture: Extreme close-up of a husked golden ear of corn with rows of plump kernels held in two hands, blurred green cornfield behind, bright sunlight

scenes.narration: But a bad harvest would finish them. All summer, they watch those stalks like their lives depend on it. They do.
scenes.caption: SUMMER, 1621
scenes.picture: A worried English settler family in plain wool and linen standing at the edge of a sunlit cornfield, looking up at a cloudless sky, dry cracked earth underfoot

scenes.narration: By autumn, it mostly works. They bring in about twenty acres of corn and six of barley and peas, though the peas mostly fail.
scenes.caption: AUTUMN HARVEST
scenes.picture: Wide golden autumn cornfield with English settlers in wool clothes carrying baskets of husked corn, a timber house and the bay in the distance, warm low sun

scenes.narration: So Governor William Bradford sends four men out hunting birds. They return with enough to feed everyone for nearly a week.
scenes.caption: FOWLING PARTY
scenes.picture: Four English men in dark coats with long matchlock guns walking back from autumn marshes with strings of ducks and geese over their shoulders, golden reeds, soft light

scenes.narration: Then Massasoit appears with about ninety Wampanoag men.
scenes.caption: 90 GUESTS
scenes.picture: A long line of Wampanoag men in deerskin mantles emerging from an autumn forest onto the hill above Plymouth, startled English settlers in dark coats looking up from their work

scenes.narration: Why did they come? Some historians think they heard the gunfire and came to check, though no source says so.
scenes.caption: WHY THEY CAME
scenes.picture: Massasoit, a proud middle-aged Wampanoag leader with a shell necklace, leading armed Wampanoag men with bows through autumn trees, alert serious faces, glancing toward distant smoke from a settlement

scenes.narration: Now there's a problem: ninety hungry guests, and a colony of barely fifty people with a small pile of food.
scenes.caption: NOT ENOUGH
scenes.picture: A flustered English woman in a linen cap and apron looks at a nearly empty wooden table with just a few dishes, while many guests wait outside the open door, worried face

scenes.narration: So the guests solve it. Massasoit's men go hunting and return carrying five deer.
scenes.caption: FIVE DEER
scenes.picture: Five Wampanoag hunters in deerskin clothes carry five deer slung on poles through autumn woods toward the settlement, proud smiles, golden leaves falling

scenes.narration: Five deer. A very welcome supply of fresh meat.
scenes.caption: VENISON
scenes.picture: Close-up of an English settler boy in a plain wool jacket staring wide-eyed at a huge roasting venison haunch turning on a spit over a fire, glowing orange light

scenes.narration: The feast lasts three days, with the settlers firing their guns, and perhaps games. And probably plenty of curious glances.
scenes.caption: THREE DAYS
scenes.picture: English settlers in dark coats firing matchlock guns into the air in a sunny clearing, Wampanoag men and children watching with curiosity, timber houses behind, white smoke drifting

scenes.narration: So what was actually on the table? Venison, mostly. Deer was the star of the show.
scenes.caption: THE MENU
scenes.picture: A long outdoor wooden table loaded with roasted deer meat on wooden platters, men and women in period clothes seated and eating, autumn trees behind

scenes.narration: Then birds: ducks, geese, and maybe wild turkey. Nobody can say for sure which.
scenes.caption: FOWL
scenes.picture: Close-up of roasted ducks and a goose on a wooden platter beside a small wild turkey, steam rising, rustic table, warm firelight

scenes.narration: Add corn dishes, probably, and possibly shellfish and eels from the bay.
scenes.caption: CORN & SEAFOOD
scenes.picture: Wooden bowls of corn porridge, flat corn bread, a heap of blue mussels and a plate of eels on a plain wooden table beside the bay, sunlit

scenes.narration: What's missing? Pumpkin pie. No butter, no wheat flour to spare, no oven, and hardly any sugar.
scenes.caption: NO PUMPKIN PIE
scenes.picture: An English woman in a linen cap staring at a small bare pumpkin on a plain table beside an empty flour sack and an empty butter crock, a simple open hearth with no oven behind her, puzzled look

scenes.narration: Cranberries grew nearby, and whether anyone served them, nobody knows. But there was no cranberry sauce as we know it.
scenes.caption: NO SAUCE
scenes.picture: Wild red cranberries growing in a boggy meadow beside the coast, a hand picking a few into a small woven basket, soft autumn light

scenes.narration: And forks? Almost nobody used them. People ate with spoons, knives, and their hands.
scenes.caption: NO FORKS
scenes.picture: Close-up of hands tearing roast meat with fingers and a knife, a wooden spoon resting in a bowl, a linen napkin over a shoulder, rustic wooden table

scenes.narration: Strangest of all, they didn't call it Thanksgiving. To them, a thanksgiving was a solemn day of prayer, not a party.
scenes.caption: NOT THANKSGIVING
scenes.picture: Pilgrims in plain dark clothes with heads bowed in prayer inside a small bare timber meeting house, light from one small window, serious faces

scenes.narration: So the meal faded away. And the next year, Tisquantum died of fever, leaving the alliance to hold without him.
scenes.picture: Tisquantum, a lean Native man with long black hair in a deerskin mantle, lying weak with fever on a bed of furs inside a wigwam, an English settler man in a dark coat sitting sadly beside him, dim firelight

scenes.narration: So how did one forgotten harvest meal become a national holiday?
scenes.caption: HOW?
scenes.picture: A festive family Thanksgiving table in a cozy wooden farmhouse, a roasted turkey, pies and a seated family in 1900s clothes, autumn leaves at the window, warm light

scenes.narration: Jump to 1863. America is tearing itself apart in the Civil War.
scenes.picture: A muddy battlefield after a battle, tattered Union soldiers in blue coats walking past broken cannons and drifting smoke, grey sky, tired faces, 1863

scenes.narration: A magazine editor named Sarah Josepha Hale has spent about seventeen years writing to presidents, begging for one national day of thanks.
scenes.caption: SARAH HALE
scenes.picture: Sarah Josepha Hale, an elderly woman with grey hair in a bun, dark Victorian dress and white lace collar, writing a letter at a desk piled with envelopes by a gas lamp, ink pot and quill

scenes.narration: Seventeen years of letters. Nothing happened. Until Abraham Lincoln.
scenes.caption: 17 YEARS
scenes.picture: Sarah Josepha Hale, an elderly woman with grey hair in a bun, dark Victorian dress and white lace collar, sitting at her desk beside a tall stack of letters, pen in hand, tired but determined face, gas lamp light

scenes.narration: In October 1863, months after the carnage at Gettysburg, he declared the last Thursday of November a day of thanksgiving.
scenes.caption: OCTOBER 1863
scenes.picture: Abraham Lincoln, a tall thin man with a dark beard and black frock coat, standing at a desk in a White House office, signing a paper with a quill, window light, serious tired face, 1863

scenes.narration: He wanted a country ripping apart to share one table, even if only for an afternoon.
scenes.caption: ONE TABLE
scenes.picture: A humble 1860s family in plain clothes sharing a simple meal around a wooden table in a candlelit farmhouse, one empty chair at the table, warm wistful mood

scenes.narration: But the Pilgrim link came from an old letter. In 1841, a historian reprinted it and called that meal the first Thanksgiving.
scenes.picture: A bespectacled historian in an 1840s dark coat sitting at a desk in a candlelit study, holding a very old brown manuscript and smiling thoughtfully, shelves of leather books behind him

scenes.narration: Schools and storybooks ran with it, and the buckled hats and pumpkin pie got added later. That's the myth, and it stuck.
scenes.caption: THE MYTH GROWS
scenes.picture: A cheerful 1890s schoolroom where children in simple clothes wear paper tall black buckled hats and paper feathers for a play, a smiling teacher in a long dark dress watching

scenes.narration: And the Wampanoag? They're still here, thousands strong, and many remember the story very differently.
scenes.caption: STILL HERE
scenes.picture: A Wampanoag family in modern everyday jackets standing together on the Massachusetts shore at sunrise, smiling softly, calm sea behind them

scenes.narration: Since 1970, some gather at Plymouth each Thanksgiving to mark a National Day of Mourning and tell their side of the story.
scenes.caption: DAY OF MOURNING
scenes.picture: A quiet group of people in warm coats standing silent on a grassy hill overlooking Plymouth harbour on a cold November morning, heads lowered, bare trees

scenes.narration: Here's the twist. The only eyewitness account of that famous meal is a single paragraph of about 115 words.
scenes.caption: 115 WORDS
scenes.picture: Close-up of a hand holding a quill above a small blank sheet of paper beside an ink pot in warm candlelight, rough timber room, soft shadows

scenes.narration: About 115 words, written by Edward Winslow. Everything else, we've stirred in ourselves.
scenes.delivery: quiet, reflective, a final wry smile
scenes.caption: WINSLOW'S LETTER
scenes.picture: Edward Winslow, an English settler man in a dark wool coat and white linen collar, seated at a rough wooden table writing with a quill by a window at golden sunset, glowing Plymouth cornfields outside

narrator: Smart, fast-talking explainer like a popular YouTube science channel, crisp and lively, never slow.

short.title: How the First Thanksgiving Really Happened
short.description:
In 1621, Pilgrims who had buried half their people hosted a feast at Plymouth. Here's how it happened, and what was really on the table.
Source: Edward Winslow's 1621 letter, Plimoth Patuxet Museums.

scenes.narration: In 1621, ninety Wampanoag men walked into a village of fifty hungry Pilgrims, and it became the first Thanksgiving.
scenes.caption: PLYMOUTH, 1621
scenes.picture: A group of Wampanoag men of 1621 with long black hair, deerskin leggings and fur mantles stepping out of a golden autumn forest toward one small thatched wooden house, a worried English settler in a wide-brimmed hat and wool coat large in the foreground watching them, tall frame.

scenes.narration: The Mayflower Pilgrims landed in the winter of 1620, and about half of them died.
scenes.caption: WINTER, 1620
scenes.picture: A grieving English woman in her thirties with a dark cloak and white linen cap kneels beside small wooden cross-shaped grave markers on a snowy hillside, a few tiny timber huts far below, grey winter dawn, sad face.

scenes.narration: Then a Native man, Samoset, walked in and said, "Welcome, Englishmen."
scenes.caption: MARCH 1621
scenes.picture: Samoset, a tall Native man with black hair, deerskin leggings and a bow on his shoulder, walks between rough timber houses raising one open friendly hand, while two startled English settlers in dark wool coats stare at him, early spring light.

scenes.narration: Samoset brought Squanto, a Wampanoag man the English once kidnapped.
scenes.caption: SQUANTO
scenes.picture: Squanto, a Wampanoag man in his forties with long black hair, a deerskin mantle and a thoughtful strong face, stands in medium shot on a grassy Plymouth hillside, grey-blue bay and a distant wooden ship behind him, spring morning.

scenes.narration: Then Wampanoag leader Massasoit made a peace pact with the Pilgrims.
scenes.caption: PEACE PACT
scenes.picture: Massasoit, a proud Wampanoag leader with a shell necklace and deerskin mantle, clasps forearms with an English leader in a dark wool coat and white collar, inside a small rough wooden room lit by a fireplace, warm firelight, two figures only.

scenes.narration: But peace doesn't fill stomachs, so Squanto taught the Pilgrims to plant corn with fish.
scenes.caption: FISH AND CORN
scenes.picture: Close-up of a Native man's brown hands pressing a silvery fish into a small mound of dark earth beside yellow corn seeds, an English settler's hand and sleeve crouching beside him, spring field, soft daylight.

scenes.narration: By autumn, the corn harvest worked, so Governor William Bradford sent men hunting.
scenes.caption: AUTUMN, 1621
scenes.picture: Governor William Bradford, an English man in his thirties with dark hair, a dark coat and wide white collar, stands proudly in a golden cornfield holding a husked ear of corn, baskets of corn at his feet, autumn sunlight, wide shot.

scenes.narration: Then Massasoit arrived with ninety men, far more guests than the colony could feed.
scenes.caption: 90 GUESTS
scenes.picture: Massasoit, a proud Wampanoag leader with a shell necklace and deerskin mantle, walks at the head of a long line of Wampanoag men in deerskin mantles emerging from an autumn forest, an astonished English woman in a linen cap in the foreground.

scenes.narration: So Massasoit's men hunted and brought back five deer.
scenes.caption: FIVE DEER
scenes.picture: Two smiling Wampanoag hunters in deerskin clothes carry a dead deer tied to a long pole on their shoulders along a path through golden autumn woods, falling leaves, warm low sun, side view.

scenes.narration: For three days they feasted together on venison and wild birds, with no pumpkin pie in sight.
scenes.caption: THREE DAYS
scenes.picture: A long rough wooden table outdoors in a 1621 village piled with roasted venison and wild ducks, English settlers in wool coats and Wampanoag men with long black hair and fur mantles eating side by side, autumn trees, seen from one end of the table.

scenes.narration: And the star of that famous table, the venison, was a gift from the guests.
scenes.caption: THE ANSWER
scenes.picture: Close view of a Wampanoag man of 1621 with long black hair and a fur mantle setting down a large roasted leg of venison on a rough wooden table in front of a smiling English settler in a wide-brimmed hat, warm evening firelight.
